opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest starting point is that synthetic data is only useful if it closes a gap you actually have. Early on, a lot of simulation work in the industry was judged on whether it looked photorealistic. We learned fairly quickly that looking good to a human and being useful to a neural network are not the same thing.

So we tried to work backwards from the perception model's failures. We'd look at where the detector or segmentation model was weak. Often it was the long tail: unusual vehicles, a person partly hidden behind a parked truck, odd lighting at dusk, construction zones that look different on every block in San Francisco. Then we'd ask whether we could generate targeted data for those cases. Waiting to encounter enough of them on the road could take months, and some of them you never want to encounter at all.

The second piece was the domain gap. A model trained on rendered images can pick up shortcuts. It might learn the texture of the renderer instead of the shape of a pedestrian. We spent a lot of effort on sensor realism, not just visual realism. That meant modeling how the actual cameras and lidar behave, including noise, motion blur, rolling shutter, lidar dropout on dark or reflective surfaces, and rain and fog effects. Getting the sensor characteristics right often mattered more than getting the textures perfect.

Third, we almost never treated synthetic data as a replacement for real data. It was a complement. The pattern that worked was to mix it with real data, or pretrain on it and fine-tune on real logs. Then we measured very carefully on real-world evaluation sets, especially on the slices we were trying to improve. If a synthetic dataset didn't move the metric on real data, it didn't matter how impressive it looked.

Increasingly, we also leaned on reconstructing real scenes from our own drives and then modifying them. You could take a real street, insert or move actors, and change the time of day. That keeps much of the real-world distribution intact while letting you create the variations you need. Neural rendering and generative methods made that much more practical over time.

The broader lesson I took away was that synthetic data is really a data engine problem, not a graphics problem. The value comes from the loop: find failures, generate targeted data, retrain, validate on reality, and repeat. The teams that treated it that way got real value out of it.

fable-5.1.text:
The honest answer is that for a long time it wasn't useful, and figuring out why was most of the work.

When I joined, the simulation team had this beautiful rendering pipeline. Photorealistic San Francisco, dynamic lighting, agents with reasonable behaviors. And the perception team basically refused to touch it. Every time they tried mixing synthetic frames into training, the model got slightly worse on real-world validation. So the synthetic data was sitting there, costing a lot of money to produce, and nobody was consuming it.

The mistake we'd been making was treating realism as the goal. We kept asking "how do we make the renders look more like camera images," and that's a bottomless pit. The question that actually unlocked things was "what does the model learn from this image that it wouldn't learn from a real one?" Framed that way, you stop caring about whether the asphalt texture is perfect and start caring about the distribution of situations.

So we flipped the strategy. Instead of trying to replace real data, we used synthetic data only for the tail. Pedestrians stepping out from behind a double-parked truck at night. A cyclist in the lane that's partially occluded by a bus. Those scenarios show up in real logs maybe a handful of times a year, so you can't learn them from fleet data alone. In simulation, you can generate ten thousand variations in an afternoon. And in those cases, a little domain gap doesn't matter as much, because the alternative is zero examples.

The second thing was being disciplined about measuring it. We built a held-out set of real events for exactly those long-tail categories, and the only thing we tracked was whether synthetic injection moved those numbers. If it helped on occluded pedestrians but cost us half a point on general detection, that was a conversation to have with actual numbers, not an argument about whether sim "feels" realistic.

And honestly, the third piece was organizational. We put a perception engineer on the simulation team for a while, and that changed what got built. The rendering team stopped optimizing for demos and started optimizing for label fidelity, sensor noise models, things that are boring to look at but matter to a model. That's the part people underestimate. The hard problem isn't rendering, it's getting the people who make the data and the people who use it to want the same thing.

r002.rationale: It describes building a held-out evaluation set, but does not say this system was built before attempts to improve the simulation or synthetic data.

r003.rationale: It identifies optimizing for photorealistic renders as the mistaken focus and says the useful goal was improving what perception models learn.

r004.rationale: It does not mention using GANs or transferring real-data characteristics onto synthetic data.

astra-6.text:
The way I’d frame it is that synthetic data has to solve a training problem, not just look convincing. You start with a weakness in the perception model: what situations does it miss, and what variation is missing from the training set? Then you generate examples around that gap, with labels that are consistent with the task.

The critical step is closing the loop with evaluation on real data. You train with the synthetic examples and check whether performance improves on held-out real-world cases. If it doesn’t, you revisit the scenarios, the realism, or the balance of synthetic and real data. Visual quality can help, but the measure of usefulness is whether the model gets better in the situations you care about.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that the goal isn’t just to generate realistic-looking images. The goal is to generate data that actually helps the perception model learn something it’s missing.

So you start with the model’s failure cases. What situations are difficult? Is it an unusual object, an occlusion, or a particular lighting condition? That gives you a much more focused target for synthetic data generation. You can vary those conditions systematically and get precise labels along with them.

Then you have to close the loop: train with that data and evaluate on held-out real-world data. If the synthetic examples look great but don’t improve performance on real examples, they’re not doing their job. The important questions become how much synthetic data to mix in, which variations matter, and whether the model is learning useful features or artifacts of the renderer.

That’s really the approach: let real-world failures guide what you generate, and let real-world evaluation tell you whether it was useful.
